title: The Decree and the Vessels
subtitle: Ezra 1:1–11
description: A Persian king's decree sends the exiles home, and the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar stole are counted out to go back with them.
paragraphs: The exile was supposed to be the end of the story, and for seventy years it looked that way. Then a Persian king who had never seen Jerusalem issued a decree about its God, and the book of Ezra opens with the reason given before the decree itself: it happened “to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia.” Jeremiah had said the exile would end. In the first year of Cyrus, the king sent a proclamation through his whole kingdom and put it in writing, and the words of a foreign emperor read like the words of a man who knew exactly whose hand was on him.

The proclamation named God before it named any policy. “The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah.” Then it opened the road home: “Whoever among you belongs to His people, may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel.” Cyrus did not merely permit the return. He framed it as his own appointment from the God of heaven, and he sent the exiles back to a city most of them had never seen, to rebuild a house their grandfathers had watched burn.

The decree also reached the people who stayed behind. “And let every survivor, wherever he lives, be assisted by the men of that region with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, along with a freewill offering for the house of God in Jerusalem.” That is the form of the decree as Ezra prints it, and it is fuller than the form Chronicles closed with: Chronicles pointed here, and here the assistance of the neighbors stands in the text itself. The response matched the command. The family heads of Judah and Benjamin rose up, with the priests and the Levites, and behind the whole list stands one quiet description of who went: it was everyone “whose spirit God had stirred.” The stirring that began in a king's spirit ran down through a people.

The neighbors did their part, supporting the travelers with articles of silver and gold, with goods and livestock and valuables, on top of the freewill offerings. Then Cyrus did something no one had a right to expect. He ordered out the articles of the house of the LORD, the very vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and set in the temple of his gods. Mithredath the treasurer brought them out and counted them, item by item, into the hand of Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah. What Babylon had taken as trophies, Persia now returned as an inventory, and every piece was numbered before it traveled.

The inventory closes the chapter, and its numbers are the point: 30 gold dishes, 1,000 silver dishes, 29 silver utensils, 30 gold bowls, 410 matching silver bowls, and 1,000 other articles. “In all, there were 5,400 gold and silver articles.” Sheshbazzar brought all of them up when the exiles went from Babylon to Jerusalem. The book that will be built out of lists and letters and decrees begins with a counted treasure and a stirred people, and the first thing it wants a reader to know is that nothing about this return was vague. God had spoken through Jeremiah. A king had put it in writing. The vessels were counted. The road home was open.

title: The Names of Those Who Came Up
subtitle: Ezra 2:1–70
description: The first return written as a register: 42,360 people, family by family and town by town, including the families who could not prove their names.
paragraphs: The second chapter of Ezra is a list, and it does not apologize for being one. A people that had been carried off as a defeated nation comes home as a register of names and numbers, family by family and town by town, because in this book being counted is what belonging looks like. “They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town,” and the list opens with the eleven leaders who walked at its head: “accompanied by Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah.” Then the count of the men of Israel begins, house by house.

The great families run into the thousands. The descendants of Senaah are the largest single house in the chapter at 3,630, then Pahath-moab at 2,812 and Parosh at 2,172, with Elam counted twice over in two branches of 1,254 each. Between the family names the towns speak up, and their numbers are smaller and more personal: the men of Bethlehem, 123; the men of Jericho, 345; the men of Bethel and Ai, 223; the men of Ramah and Geba, 621. Some of these places had not heard their own names called in an Israelite census for seventy years. The list reads them back into the land one count at a time, and it refuses to round any of them away.

Then come the men of the house itself. Four priestly houses return: Jedaiah with 973, Immer with 1,052, Pashhur with 1,247, and Harim with 1,017. Against their thousands the Levites are startlingly few, only 74 in the whole company, with 128 singers of the sons of Asaph and 139 gatekeepers. The temple servants and the descendants of the servants of Solomon, the hereditary workers of the house, are counted with the same care as the priests: “The temple servants and descendants of the servants of Solomon numbered 392 in all.” Nobody in this chapter is too small to be numbered, and nobody's nearness to the altar changes the care with which they are written down.

The list is honest about its gaps. A company of 652 came up from towns in Babylon but could not prove their families were descended from Israel, and among the priests three houses searched for their records and failed: “These men searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean.” Even that exclusion was handled with patience rather than finality. “The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim.” The door was shut, but it was shut in a way that left it to God to open. A list that exists to say who belongs turns out to be just as careful about who cannot yet be shown to belong.

The chapter ends with its totals, and the totals are the homecoming in one sum: “The whole assembly numbered 42,360,” besides 7,337 menservants and maidservants and 200 singers, with 736 horses, 245 mules, 435 camels, and 6,720 donkeys. When they reached the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, the family heads gave freewill offerings to rebuild it on its original site: “According to their ability, they gave to the treasury for this work 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priestly garments.” Then the list dissolves into ordinary life, which was the whole purpose of it. The priests, the Levites, the singers, the gatekeepers, the temple servants, and all Israel settled in their own towns.

title: The Altar and the Weeping Foundation
subtitle: Ezra 3:1–13
description: The altar is rebuilt and the feasts resume before the temple has a foundation, and when the foundation is laid, joy and weeping rise in one sound.
paragraphs: By the seventh month the returned exiles had settled in their towns, and then they did the thing that turned a migration back into a nation: “the people assembled as one man in Jerusalem.” The temple was a ruin and its foundation was not yet laid, but Jeshua son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his associates, knew where worship starts. Before walls, before a foundation, they built the altar of the God of Israel, to sacrifice burnt offerings on it “as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God.” The first structure of the second temple was not the temple. It was an altar standing in the open.

They set the altar on its foundation and began the morning and evening burnt offerings, and the text refuses to hide the atmosphere in which they did it: they offered “even though they feared the people of the land.” Worship resumed under fear, in a roofless ruin, surrounded by neighbors who did not wish them well. Then, still with no temple standing, they kept the Feast of Tabernacles as it is written, with the burnt offerings counted out day by day as prescribed. After that came the regular burnt offerings, the New Moons, and all the appointed feasts of the LORD, along with the freewill offerings. The calendar of Israel started turning again before the house that calendar belonged to existed.

The text marks the order on purpose. On the first day of the seventh month the offerings began, although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid. Sacrifice did not wait for architecture. Only then did the building money move: payment to the masons and carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the men of Sidon and Tyre to float cedar logs from Lebanon down the sea to Joppa, the same supply line Solomon had used, now running again under the authorization of Cyrus king of Persia. In the second month of the second year after their arrival, the work formally began, and Levites twenty years old and up were appointed to supervise the construction of the house of God.

When the builders laid the foundation, the returned community staged the moment the way David had prescribed it generations earlier. The priests took their positions in their apparel, with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, stood with cymbals to praise the LORD. They sang responsively, answering one another with praise and thanksgiving: “For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever.” Then all the people shouted, a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid. It was only a foundation, a footprint of a building, and they treated its laying like a victory.

But the shout was not the only sound, and Ezra's account is too honest to clean it up. Many of the older priests and Levites and family heads, men who had seen the first temple before it burned, wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this one, while many others shouted for joy. Both sounds rose at once and neither could be separated from the other: “The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping,” because the people were making so much noise, and the sound was heard from afar. Grief for what was lost and joy at what was beginning stood in the same crowd, at the same foundation, and the book lets them stay mixed.

title: Letters That Stopped the Work
subtitle: Ezra 4:1–24
description: A refused partnership turns into hired counselors and royal letters, and the work on the house of God is stopped by force.
paragraphs: The foundation had barely been laid when the first opposition arrived wearing a friendly face. The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the exiles were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel, and they came to Zerubbabel and the heads of the families with an offer: “Let us build with you because, like you, we seek your God and have been sacrificing to Him since the time of King Esar-haddon of Assyria, who brought us here.” The answer was flat and immediate: “You have no part with us in building a house for our God, since we alone must build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.” The refused partnership did not go home quietly. From that day the people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build.

Frustration became a profession. “They hired counselors against them to frustrate their plans” throughout the reign of Cyrus and down to the reign of Darius, and the chapter now does something a reader has to notice: it gathers the opposition of later years into this one telling, the way a file gathers letters written across a generation. An accusation was lodged at the beginning of the reign of Xerxes. In the days of Artaxerxes, officials wrote again, and their letter against Jerusalem is the one the chapter prints in full. The kings are not re-sorted into a tidier order here; the letters stand in the file in the order the book gives them, a record of how long and how patiently this small work was opposed.

The letter from Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe, written for the officials and peoples settled west of the Euphrates, is a skilled piece of alarm. “Let it be known to the king that the Jews who came from you to us have returned to Jerusalem and are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city.” Then it aimed at the treasury: “if that city is rebuilt and its walls are restored, they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer.” Its strongest argument was history. Search the record books of your fathers, the writers urged, and you will find this city rebellious from ancient times, harmful to kings, destroyed for exactly that reason. It was, point for point, a true account of Jerusalem's past, aimed like a weapon at Jerusalem's future.

Artaxerxes answered as the letter hoped. The records were searched, and the king reported the result himself: “It was discovered that this city has revolted against kings from ancient times, engaging in rebellion and sedition.” Mighty kings had ruled there and drawn tribute from the whole region. So the decree went out: “issue an order for these men to stop, so that this city will not be rebuilt until I so order.” The warning that closed it had the empire's full weight behind it: see that you do not neglect this matter, and do not let the threat grow at the royal expense. It is worth noticing what the letter and the decree were about: the city and its walls, in a later king's reign. The book files them here, inside the temple's story, because their effect landed on the builders all the same.

The effect was immediate. When the text of the king's letter was read to Rehum and Shimshai and their associates, they hurried to Jerusalem and stopped the Jews by force. “Thus the construction of the house of God in Jerusalem ceased, and it remained at a standstill until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.” The altar stood, the foundation lay in the open, and above both of them hung a royal order that said stop. The book does not soften the length of that silence. The work of God in Jerusalem was halted by paperwork and soldiers, and it stayed halted until a new king sat on the throne and two prophets, whose books stand earlier in this series, lifted their voices in the street.

title: The Eye of Their God
subtitle: Ezra 5:1–17
description: Two prophets restart the work, a governor writes a fair report, and everything rides on whether a dead king's decree can be found in the archives.
paragraphs: The restart did not come from a palace. It came from two preachers. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them, and their sermons are not repeated here, because they stand whole in their own books in this series. What Ezra records is the effect: Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up and began again to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. “And the prophets of God were with them, helping them.” Scaffolding went back up around a foundation that had sat unfinished for years, and this time the builders did not stop when the officials arrived.

The officials came quickly. Tattenai, governor of the whole region west of the Euphrates, arrived with Shethar-bozenai and their associates and put two questions to the Jews: who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure, and what are the names of the men constructing this building? It was the opening of an imperial investigation, the same machinery that had stopped the work before. But the outcome this time is explained in one sentence before the paperwork even begins: “But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, so that they were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned.” The builders kept building while the empire wrote its letters.

Tattenai's report to King Darius is the surprise of the chapter, because it is fair. He describes what his own eyes saw in the province of Judah, at the house of the great God: “The people are rebuilding it with large stones and placing timbers in the walls. This work is being carried out diligently and is prospering in their hands.” No accusation, no inflated threat, no hired alarm. He reports that he questioned the elders about their authority and asked for their leaders' names, and then he passes their answer up the chain exactly as they gave it. The machinery that once ran on a slanted letter now runs on a straight one, and the difference matters to everything that follows.

The elders' answer is a history lesson in four sentences. “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the temple that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and completed.” Then the confession: “But since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon,” who destroyed the temple and carried the people away. Then the turn: in the first year of his reign, Cyrus issued a decree to rebuild this house of God, removed the gold and silver articles from the temple of Babylon, and gave them to Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor, with orders to put them in the temple in Jerusalem and let the house be rebuilt on its original site. Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation, they conclude, and from that time until now it has been under construction, but it has not yet been completed.

So the chapter ends not with a verdict but with a request, and Tattenai makes it himself: “let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon to see if King Cyrus did indeed issue a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” Then let the king send his decision. Everything now rides on a scroll in a treasury, on whether a dead king's decree can be found in his own archives. The builders build on, the letter travels east, and the question hanging over the house of God is not whether God authorized it. It is whether Persia can find its own paperwork.

title: The House Finished and the Passover Kept
subtitle: Ezra 6:1–22
description: Darius finds Cyrus' scroll, funds the work from the royal treasury, and the finished house is dedicated and Passover is kept with joy.
paragraphs: King Darius ordered the search Tattenai had asked for, and the archives of Babylon were opened. The scroll was not found in Babylon. It turned up in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media, a memorandum from the first year of the empire, and its words settled the question that had hung over the building site: “In the first year of King Cyrus, he issued a decree concerning the house of God in Jerusalem: Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices, and let its foundations be firmly laid.” The memorandum gave the house its dimensions, sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide, three layers of cut stones and one of timbers, the costs paid from the royal treasury. It also ordered the gold and silver articles Nebuchadnezzar had taken to be returned to the temple in Jerusalem and deposited in the house of God. Tattenai's question had been whether Cyrus really issued such a decree. He did, and it was on file.

Darius did not merely confirm the old decree. He issued a new one, and it reversed the whole posture of the empire toward the builders. To Tattenai and his officials the command began with distance: “You must stay away from that place!” Then came the order no governor west of the Euphrates had ever been given about this work: “Leave this work on the house of God alone. Let the governor and elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its original site.” The investigation that was supposed to test the builders' authority ended with the investigators ordered off the site.

The decree then put the royal treasury behind the work it had once been used to stop. The cost was to be paid in full to the elders from the royal treasury, out of the taxes of the provinces west of the Euphrates, “so that the work will not be hindered.” Whatever the priests in Jerusalem requested for the burnt offerings to the God of heaven, “young bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven,” along with wheat, salt, wine, and oil, “must be given to them daily without fail,” so that the people could offer sacrifices of a sweet aroma to the God of heaven and pray for the lives of the king and his sons. The empire was now funding the prayers of the returned exiles, daily, as a matter of royal policy.

Darius also gave his decree teeth. If any man interfered with the directive, “a beam is to be torn from his house and raised up, and he is to be impaled on it,” and his house was to be made a pile of rubble for the offense. Then the king closed with a curse aimed at his own successors: “May God, who has caused His Name to dwell there, overthrow any king or people who lifts a hand to alter this decree or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem.” And he signed it like a man who expected compliance: “I, Darius, have issued the decree. Let it be carried out with diligence.” Tattenai, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates carried it out with exactly that diligence. The machinery of Persia, which had stopped the work by letter, now protected it by letter.

So the elders built and prospered, carried by the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah and backed by the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, and the long standstill ended in a finished house: “And this temple was completed on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius.” The people of Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the rest of the exiles dedicated it with joy, offering a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering for all Israel, one for each tribe. The priests and Levites were appointed to their divisions for the service of God in Jerusalem, as written in the Book of Moses. Then, on the fourteenth day of the first month, the exiles kept the Passover, all of them ceremonially clean. “The Israelites who had returned from exile ate it, together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel.” For seven days they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread with joy, “because the LORD had made them joyful and turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them to strengthen their hands in the work on the house of the God of Israel.” That is the name the text itself gives the Persian king, and the joy is the last word of the first return.

title: The Scribe Who Set His Heart
subtitle: Ezra 7:1–28
description: Many years later, a scribe who set his heart to study the Law, practice it, and teach it comes up from Babylon carrying a king's letter.
paragraphs: “Many years later, during the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra son of Seraiah” steps into his own book, and the text marks the size of the step with nothing more than those opening words. The finished temple of the last episode is decades in the past. In the interval this opening steps over, another story unfolded at Susa under King Xerxes, the story of Esther, which stands next in this series in its own book. Here the line of the return runs on, and it runs now through one man. Ezra's ancestry is traced up through Seraiah, Azariah, Hilkiah, Zadok, and Phinehas, all the way to “the son of Aaron the chief priest.” The priesthood that the exile scattered is about to walk back into Jerusalem in a single person's genealogy.

The introduction the book gives him is compact enough to memorize: “this Ezra came up from Babylon. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses, which the LORD, the God of Israel, had given.” The king had granted Ezra all his requests, the text says, “for the hand of the LORD his God was upon him.” That phrase becomes the second movement's refrain. Ezra came up in the seventh year of Artaxerxes with priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants, beginning the journey from Babylon on the first day of the first month and arriving in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month, “for the gracious hand of his God was upon him.” Four months of road, and the book accounts for the safe arrival with the hand, not the escort.

Between the introduction and the journey stands the verse the whole book turns on, the man's own program stated once and then simply enacted: “For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel.” Study, practice, teach, in that order. Everything Ezra does in the rest of the book is one of those three verbs at work: he studies on the road, he practices in the weighing and the fast, and he teaches in the assembly still to come. Readers who want to know what Ezra is, before they watch what Ezra does, are given this sentence and nothing flashier.

He did not travel on goodwill alone. Artaxerxes gave him a letter, and the book prints it as the document it is: “Artaxerxes, king of kings. To Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven: Greetings.” The letter decrees that any volunteers among the Israelites in the kingdom, priests and Levites included, may go up with Ezra to Jerusalem. Ezra is sent by the king and his seven counselors to evaluate Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of his God, which is in his hand, and he carries the silver and gold the king and his counselors freely offered to the God of Israel, plus whatever the province of Babylon contributes in freewill offerings. The money is for bulls, rams, and lambs and their offerings for the altar, and the king's treasurers west of the Euphrates are ordered to supply whatever more Ezra requires, “up to a hundred talents of silver, a hundred cors of wheat, a hundred baths of wine, a hundred baths of olive oil, and salt without limit.”

The letter's last charge makes the scribe a judge: “And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God, which you possess, are to appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people west of the Euphrates,” and to teach the laws of his God to anyone who does not know them, with strict judgment, death or banishment or confiscation or imprisonment, for whoever refuses the law of God and the law of the king. No tribute, duty, or toll may be imposed on any priest, Levite, singer, doorkeeper, temple servant, or servant of the house of God. Then the book changes voice, and the change is the point: the letter ends, and Ezra speaks for the first time. “Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put into the heart of the king to so honor the house of the LORD in Jerusalem.” Favor had come to him before the king, his counselors, and all his powerful officials. His own words for what the favor produced: “And because the hand of the LORD my God was upon me, I took courage and gathered the leaders of Israel to return with me.” From here to the end of the book, the story is told in the first person by the man at its center.

title: The Fast at the Ahava
subtitle: Ezra 8:1–36
description: Ezra's company fasts at the Ahava instead of asking for soldiers, and the treasure is weighed out at the river and weighed in at the house.
paragraphs: Ezra tells the journey in his own voice, and he begins it the way this book begins everything, with a list: “These are the family heads and genealogical records of those who returned with me from Babylon during the reign of King Artaxerxes.” The heads of the families are named with their counts. Gershom from the descendants of Phinehas, Daniel from Ithamar, Hattush from the line of David. Zechariah of Parosh with 150 men registered beside him, Eliehoenai of Pahath-Moab with 200, Shecaniah of Zattu with 300, Ebed of Adin with 50, Jeshaiah of Elam with 70, Zebadiah of Shephatiah with 80, Obadiah of Joab with 218, Shelomith of Bani with 160, another Zechariah of Bebai with 28, Johanan of Azgad with 110, the later sons of Adonikam with 60, and Uthai and Zaccur of Bigvai with 70. It is a smaller company than the first return, and every man in it is counted anyway.

At the canal that flows to Ahava, Ezra assembled them and camped three days, and the inspection turned up the company's great lack: “And when I searched among the people and priests, I found no Levites there.” The house they were traveling to serve had almost no servants of Levi in the caravan. Ezra did not shrug and march. He summoned nine leaders and two teachers and sent them to Iddo, the leader at Casiphia, carrying a message for Iddo and his kinsmen, the temple servants there, to send ministers for the house of God. “And since the gracious hand of our God was upon us, they brought us Sherebiah,” a man of insight from the descendants of Mahli, with his sons and brothers, eighteen men, and Hashabiah and Jeshaiah of Merari with twenty more, and 220 temple servants, “all designated by name.” The hand of God, in this chapter, looks like a recruiting trip that worked.

Then the caravan did the most impractical thing in the whole book, on purpose. “And there by the Ahava Canal I proclaimed a fast, so that we might humble ourselves before our God and ask Him for a safe journey for us and our children, with all our possessions.” Ezra states the reason with a candor few leaders would put in writing: “For I was ashamed to ask the king for an escort of soldiers and horsemen to protect us from our enemies on the road, since we had told him, ‘The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him.’” He had preached God's protection to the king of Persia. Asking that king for cavalry now would unsay the sermon. “So we fasted and petitioned our God about this, and He granted our request.” The treasure caravan crossed hostile country with a fast for an escort.

Before the march, the treasure was weighed out in public. Ezra set apart twelve of the leading priests, with Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers, and weighed into their hands the contribution of the king, his counselors, his leaders, and all the Israelites present: 650 talents of silver, articles of silver weighing 100 talents, 100 talents of gold, 20 gold bowls valued at 1,000 darics, and two articles of fine polished bronze, “as precious as gold.” His charge to the carriers made the cargo a trust, not a shipment: “You are holy to the LORD, and these articles are holy. The silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers.” And then the instruction that gives the chapter its shape: “Guard them carefully until you weigh them out in the chambers of the house of the LORD in Jerusalem.” Weighed out at the river, weighed in at the house. Nothing in between was left to trust.

They set out from the Ahava Canal on the twelfth day of the first month, and the hand of their God was upon them, protecting them from enemies and bandits along the way. In Jerusalem they rested three days. On the fourth day, in the house of God, the silver and gold and sacred articles were weighed into the hand of Meremoth son of Uriah the priest, with Eleazar son of Phinehas and the Levites beside him, and the audit closed exactly as the charge had required: “Everything was verified by number and weight, and the total weight was recorded at that time.” Then the returned exiles offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel, 12 bulls for all Israel, 96 rams, 77 lambs, and 12 male goats for a sin offering, and delivered the king's edicts to the royal satraps and governors west of the Euphrates, who proceeded to assist the people and the house of God. The scribe was home, the treasure was counted, and the Law he carried was still unopened in public. That was about to change, and not the way he had planned.

title: The Prayer at the Evening Offering
subtitle: Ezra 9:1–15
description: The leaders' report of mixed marriages drives Ezra to his knees, and his prayer confesses everything and asks for nothing.
paragraphs: The report reached Ezra after the journey was complete and the offerings were made, and it came from the leaders themselves: “The people of Israel, including the priests and Levites, have not kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples” whose practices the report names with the old list, Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites. The charge was specific. Israelite men had taken daughters of the peoples of the land as wives for themselves and their sons. And the detail that made it a crisis of the whole return, not a private failing, came at the end of the report: “Indeed, the Israelites have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and their sons, so that the holy seed has been mixed with the people of the land. And the leaders and officials have taken the lead in this unfaithfulness!” The men charged with guarding the separation had led the breach of it.

Ezra's response was physical before it was verbal. “When I heard this report, I tore my tunic and cloak, pulled out some hair from my head and beard, and sat down in horror.” He did not call a meeting or draft a policy. He sat in the ruin of his own clothing while everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around him, and he stayed sitting in horror until the evening offering. The scribe who had crossed an empire with the Law in his hand had arrived to find the returned community already entangled with the peoples the Law warned against, and his first recorded act in Jerusalem after the audit of the treasure was grief that lasted all day.

At the evening offering he rose from his humiliation, his tunic and cloak still torn, fell on his knees, and spread out his hands to the LORD his God. The prayer that follows is the longest speech in the book, and it is confession all the way down, with no request in it at all. It opens in shame: “O my God, I am ashamed and embarrassed to lift up my face to You, my God, because our iniquities are higher than our heads, and our guilt has reached the heavens.” Ezra does not pray about them. The iniquities are ours, the guilt is ours, and the history he recites is one long sentence of consequence: “Because of our iniquities, we and our kings and priests have been delivered into the hands of the kings of the earth,” subjected to the sword, to captivity, to pillage and humiliation, from the days of the fathers to this day.

Then the prayer turns, and the turn is what makes it devastating. “But now, for a brief moment, grace has come from the LORD our God to preserve for us a remnant and to give us a stake in His holy place.” In bondage God had not forsaken them: “Though we are slaves, our God has not forsaken us in our bondage, but He has extended to us grace in the sight of the kings of Persia,” giving them new life to rebuild the house of God and repair its ruins, and a wall of protection in Judah and Jerusalem. Against that grace Ezra sets the command they have broken, the word given through the prophets about the land: “do not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters for your sons. Never seek their peace or prosperity, so that you may be strong and may eat the good things of the land,” and leave it as an inheritance to your sons forever. Grace received, commandments forsaken, in that order, is the whole prayer in miniature.

The closing movement asks the question the whole chapter has been building and then refuses to answer it for God. God has punished them less than their iniquities deserve, Ezra says, “though You, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserve and have given us such a remnant as this.” So: “shall we again break Your commandments and intermarry with the peoples who commit these abominations?” Would God not be angry enough to wipe them out, leaving no remnant or survivor? The prayer ends standing in the guilt it confesses, with no plea for an exception: “O LORD, God of Israel, You are righteous! For we remain this day as a remnant. Here we are before You in our guilt, though because of it no one can stand before You.” The evening offering rose that day next to a kneeling scribe who asked for nothing, and the book lets the confession hang in the air unanswered, because the answer, when it comes, will come from the people.

title: The Assembly in the Rain
subtitle: Ezra 10:1–44
description: A covenant is sworn, an assembly trembles in the rain, an investigation sits for three months, and the book ends on its list.
paragraphs: The prayer did what the fast at the Ahava had done: it gathered a crowd. While Ezra prayed and made this confession, “weeping and falling facedown before the house of God, a very large assembly of Israelites” gathered around him, men, women, and children, and the people wept bitterly as well. Into that weeping the first proposal came, not from Ezra but from a man named Shecaniah son of Jehiel, of the descendants of Elam. He stated the guilt without trimming it: “We have been unfaithful to our God by marrying foreign women from the people of the land, yet in spite of this, there is hope for Israel.” Hope, in his sentence, is not the denial of the guilt. It is what stands on the far side of acting on it.

The proposal was a covenant. “So now let us make a covenant before our God to send away all the foreign wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the command of our God.” Let it be done according to the Law, he said, and then he turned the responsibility back to the kneeling scribe: “Get up, for this matter is your responsibility, and we will support you. Be strong and take action!” Ezra got up. He made the leading priests, the Levites, and all Israel take an oath to do what had been said, and they took the oath. Then he withdrew from before the house of God to the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib and stayed there without food or water, “because he was mourning over the unfaithfulness of the exiles.” The covenant had been sworn. Carrying it out would take a winter.

A proclamation went through Judah and Jerusalem: every exile was to gather at Jerusalem within three days, and whoever failed to appear would forfeit all his property and be expelled from the assembly of the exiles. So on the twentieth day of the ninth month the whole company sat in the square at the house of God, “trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain.” Ezra the priest stood and put the charge to them directly: “You have been unfaithful by marrying foreign women, adding to the guilt of Israel.” Then the instruction: “Now, therefore, make a confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers, and do His will. Separate yourselves from the people of the land and from your foreign wives.” The assembly answered in one loud voice: “Truly we must do as you say!”

But the same assembly, standing in the rain it was trembling from, named the practical truth: there were too many people, it was the rainy season, they could not stay out in the open, and this was not the work of one or two days, for the transgression was great. Their counter-proposal was procedure, not refusal: let the leaders represent the whole assembly, and let every man in every town who had married a foreign woman come at an appointed time with the elders and judges of his town, until the fierce anger of God in this matter turned away. Only two men, Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah, supported by Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite, opposed the plan, and the text records their opposition and moves on. The exiles did as proposed. Ezra selected family heads by name to sit for their families, the investigation opened on the first day of the tenth month, and by the first day of the first month they had dealt with every man who had married a foreign woman.

What remains of the book is the record of that investigation, a list, like the list the book opened with, but this one reads in the other direction. It begins with the priests: among the descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers were Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah, who pledged to send their wives away and presented a ram from the flock as a guilt offering. Then the descendants of Immer, of Harim, of Pashhur; then the Levites, the singer Eliashib, the gatekeepers Shallum, Telem, and Uri; then Israelite family after Israelite family, Parosh, Elam, Zattu, Bebai, Bani, Pahath-moab, Harim, Hashum, Binnui, Nebo, name after name, each one a household. The book that began with a counted treasure and a counted people ends with a counted guilt, and its final sentence is the list's own summary, left exactly where the text leaves it: “All these men had married foreign women, and some of them had children by these wives.” There is no epilogue after it. The return story does not close here; it stands open, and the next voice in this series is Nehemiah's.
